knowledge_graph.title: Salmonella enterica
knowledge_graph.description: Salmonella enterica is a rod-shaped, flagellate, facultative anaerobic, Gram-negative bacterium and a species of the genus Salmonella. It is divided into six subspecies, arizonae, diarizonae, houtenae (IV), salamae (II), indica (VI), and enterica (I).

text_blocks.snippet: Salmonella enterica can cause a variety of illnesses, most commonly gastroenteritis (diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and fever), but also more serious conditions like enteric fever (including typhoid fever), bacteremia, and extraintestinal infections. These infections can range from mild and self-limiting to severe and life-threatening, especially in vulnerable populations like young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals.
snippet_highlighted_words: gastroenteritis (diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and fever), but also more serious conditions like enteric fever (including typhoid fever), bacteremia, and extraintestinal infections

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a breakdown of the diseases caused by Salmonella enterica:

list.snippet: This is the most common form of salmonella infection, characterized by diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever.
Symptoms usually appear within 12 to 72 hours after exposure and can last for 4 to 7 days.
Most cases are mild and resolve without treatment, but dehydration can be a concern, especially in young children and the elderly.
These are more severe systemic illnesses characterized by prolonged fever, headache, abdominal pain, and sometimes a rash.

Typhoid fever, caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi, is particularly dangerous and can lead to complications like intestinal perforation, hemorrhage, and neurological problems if left untreated.
Paratyphoid fever, caused by Salmonella enterica serotypes Paratyphi A, B, or C, has similar symptoms but is generally less severe.
Salmonella can spread beyond the intestines, leading to bacteremia (bacteria in the bloodstream).
This can result in infections in other parts of the body, including bones (osteomyelitis), joints (infectious arthritis), heart valves (endocarditis), and the central nervous system (meningitis).
These infections are more likely to occur in individuals with weakened immune systems or certain underlying medical conditions.
Some individuals can become asymptomatic carriers of Salmonella, meaning they carry the bacteria in their bodies without experiencing symptoms.
They can still shed the bacteria and transmit it to others.
Reactive arthritis: An inflammatory response that can affect the joints, eyes, and urinary tract after a Salmonella infection.
Sepsis: A life-threatening condition caused by the body's overwhelming response to infection.
Myocarditis, encephalopathy, and intravascular coagulation: Rare but serious complications that can occur in severe cases.
